newsitem.title: CHINA: China central bank seen checking yuan's rise.
newsitem.headline: China central bank seen checking yuan's rise.

text.p: China's currency is gaining on the back of a strong trade surplus, falling inflation and high foreign investment, but the central bank is intervening at every step to slow its rise, bankers said on Thursday.

The central People's Bank of China was determined to maintain the yuan's stability against the dollar mainly because there were no mechanisms available to allow Chinese banks and exporters to hedge currency risk, the bankers said.
Its efforts have been successful. The yuan, or renminbi, is one of the world's most stable currencies against the dollar, the unit upon which most Chinese trade is conducted.
But with the dollar hitting a 42-month high against the yen late last month and nearing its 1996 high against the mark, the yuan has appreciated sharply against other major currencies.

"The central bank wants a stable exchange rate and manages it through the Shanghai foreign exchange market," a Chinese banker said. "Chinese banks and firms can't handle fluctuations like those in the dollar or yen. They don't have the tools to hedge currency risk."
The yuan closed on Thursday on the Shanghai-based foreign exchange market at $8.3008 to the dollar, up from 8.32 in May and 8.7 in January 1994.
"The central bank will not let the yuan rise higher than 8.2591, its record high (since the Shanghai foreign exchange market opened in April 1994)," he said. The yuan set its high on May 15, 1995.
A foreign banker said that there had been a dramatic change in perception of the yuan in the last 12 months.
"A year ago, multinationals were forecasting a 10 percent depreciation in the yuan a year over the next five to 10 years," he said. "This view must change."
The factors pushing the yuan up are a sharp fall in inflation, a huge trade surplus, record foreign exchange reserves and large inward investment.

Vice Premier Zhu Rongji said on Wednesday that nationwide retail prices in 1996 would rise about 6.5 percent, down from 14.8 percent in 1995, and that foreign exchange reserves would exceed $100 billion by year-end, up from $73.597 billion at the end of 1995.
In the first 10 months of this year, China posted a trade surplus of $12.01 billion against a surplus of $16.7 billion for all of 1995.
In the first nine months of 1996, China attracted $29.2 billion in direct foreign investment, against $37.7 billion in all of 1995, official figures show.
The foreign banker said that all these factors put upward pressure on the yuan, with the main downward factor of 1995 -- inflation -- now removed.
But he said control of the yuan remained with the central bank despite trading on the Shanghai foreign exchange interbank market.

"The management of the exchange rate is all in the hands of SAEC (State Administration of Exchange Control, part of the central bank)," he said. "The market is not allowed to speculate and exporters have to surrender all their foreign exchange earnings to state banks.
"The entry of fast money is not permitted. There is an insulation of the domestic monetary system from the external system," he said.
In a front-page analysis on Thursday, the Shanghai-based Business News said Chinese firms did not have the flexibility of foreign firms in dealing with big fluctuations in exchange rates.
